body:
Thrust comes from expelling material

A rocket engine moves a vehicle by expelling matter in one direction, causing the rocket to experience a force in the opposite direction. This follows Newton's 3rd law of motion: forces between 2 interacting bodies are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction. The backward-moving exhaust and the forward-moving rocket gain momentum in opposite directions.

Thrust is the force produced by a propulsion system to move or change the motion of a vehicle. It is measured in newtons (N) or kilonewtons (kN).

A rocket does not push against the surrounding air. It can operate in the vacuum of space because the reaction involves the rocket and the material it ejects. A rocket launching from Earth must develop large thrust quickly to overcome gravity, whereas a satellite already in orbit may need only a small thrust to adjust its path.

What is a propellant?

A propellant is material carried or supplied to an engine and expelled to produce thrust. In a chemical rocket, energy stored in chemicals produces hot gases which leave the engine at high speed. A typical bipropellant rocket uses 2 separately stored substances: a fuel, which releases chemical energy when it reacts, and an oxidiser, which supports the reaction. Unlike an ordinary flame that uses oxygen from the air, such a rocket carries its oxidiser, enabling combustion in space.

A monopropellant thruster instead stores 1 prepared propellant, which can release hot gases through a suitable chemical reaction or decomposition. It need not have separate fuel and oxidiser tanks. Electric thrusters use a different energy source: electrical power accelerates expelled propellant without relying on chemical combustion.

Thrust and propellant efficiency are not the same

High thrust means a large force is available at a given moment. High specific impulse, usually expressed in seconds, means a propulsion system uses propellant efficiently to produce a change in motion. A system can have excellent propellant efficiency but very low thrust. This distinction explains why a heavy launch vehicle commonly uses chemical propulsion, while a satellite may benefit from electric propulsion operating over a long time.

Prelims focus

  • Rocket thrust results from backward ejection of matter and forward reaction force.
  • Newton's 3rd law describes equal and opposite forces acting on different bodies.
  • Bipropellant systems use a fuel and an oxidiser; monopropellant systems store 1 prepared propellant.
  • Specific impulse indicates propellant efficiency; thrust indicates force.
  • Trap: A rocket does not need atmospheric oxygen or air to push against when operating in space.

[NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 9, 'Force and Laws of Motion', printed pp. 122-125 (2018-19); NCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter 6, 'Combustion and Flame', printed pp. 64-68 (2018-19); NASA, '4.0 In-Space Propulsion', sections 4.5-4.6 (consulted 4 November 2026).]

pictures.caption: A launch vehicle must produce enough thrust to rise against gravity.

title: How rocket propulsion works: thrust, propellants and efficiency

body:
Meaning of semi-cryogenic propulsion

Cryogenic means kept at an extremely low temperature so that a substance remains liquid. In a semi-cryogenic rocket engine, the usual propellant combination is liquid oxygen (LOX) and refined kerosene. Oxygen is stored as a cryogenic liquid, but kerosene is a liquid that does not require cryogenic storage under ordinary conditions. The prefix semi refers to this difference in propellant storage, not to a rocket that is only partly powered.

The kerosene is the fuel and LOX is the oxidiser. When they react, the engine produces hot gases which are expelled through a nozzle to generate thrust. Because the engine carries oxygen, it can work beyond the atmosphere. Kerosene is much denser and simpler to store than liquid hydrogen, while LOX still requires very cold storage.

How it differs from a fully cryogenic engine

TypeTypical propellantsWhat needs very cold storage?
Fully cryogenicLiquid hydrogen (LH2) and LOXBoth hydrogen and oxygen
Semi-cryogenicRefined kerosene and LOXOxygen; not the kerosene
Earth-storable liquidStored liquid fuel and oxidiser, such as hydrazine-derived fuel and nitrogen tetroxideNeither normally needs cryogenic refrigeration

All 3 rows describe chemical propulsion. The choice affects propellant storage, handling, mass and rocket performance. A semi-cryogenic engine offers a practical combination of high thrust and relatively compact fuel storage. It is not an electric engine, and using LOX does not mean the engine runs without a fuel.

ISRO's SE2000 engine and SC120 stage

ISRO's Liquid Propulsion Systems Centre (LPSC) is developing the SE2000 semi-cryogenic engine, in the 2000 kN thrust class. Its intended fuel is rocket-grade refined kerosene called Isrosene, paired with LOX. The proposed SC120 stage is intended to replace the existing L110 liquid core stage of the LVM3 launch vehicle. ISRO has described a further LVM3 upgrade combining SC120 with an uprated C32 cryogenic upper stage to improve payload capacity.

Development testing must be distinguished from an operational launch. A Power Head Test Article (PHTA) contains the engine systems except the thrust chamber. ISRO reported the first successful PHTA hot test on 28 March 2025, followed by a 175-tonne (88%) test on 24 June 2026. On 5 September 2026, ISRO announced that the PHTA had completed its 9th hot test at IPRC, Mahendragiri, Tamil Nadu. It reached the 200-tonne thrust-equivalent level (100% of the planned rating) during a 35-second test, including 5 seconds at that level. This was a test of an intermediate engine configuration, not proof that a complete SE2000 engine or SC120 stage had flown.

ISRO describes LOX and Isrosene as cleaner and less toxic than conventional hydrazine-based propellants. However, kerosene contains carbon, so its combustion is not emission-free. Semi-cryogenic identifies the propellant-temperature arrangement; green is a separate assessment of environmental and handling characteristics.

Prelims focus

  • Semi-cryogenic propellants: LOX (oxidiser) and refined kerosene or Isrosene (fuel).
  • Fully cryogenic pair: LOX and LH2.
  • SE2000: planned 2000 kN-class engine; SC120: proposed LVM3 stage replacing L110.
  • LPSC develops the system; IPRC, Mahendragiri, conducts tests.
  • 5 September 2026: the PHTA reached its 200-tonne full-rating test level, not an operational flight milestone.
  • Trap: Do not confuse the semi-cryogenic SC120 stage with the cryogenic C32 upper stage.

[ISRO, 'ISRO achieves major breakthrough in Semicryogenic Engine development', 28 March 2025; ISRO, 'ISRO successfully conducted hot test of Semicryogenic Engine Power Head Test Article at higher thrust level', 27 June 2026; ISRO, 'ISRO successfully conducts hot test of Semicryogenic Engine Power Head Test Article at full thrust level', 5 September 2026; LPSC, 'Advanced Propulsion Systems', semi-cryogenic section (all consulted 4 November 2026).]

pictures.caption: Ground testing is a development milestone, not a flight of the finished stage.

title: Semi-cryogenic propulsion: liquid oxygen, kerosene and the SC120 stage

body:
Using electricity instead of combustion

Electric propulsion uses electrical energy to accelerate propellant and eject it at high speed, producing a reaction force on a spacecraft. The electricity may come from solar panels and the spacecraft's electrical system. Unlike a chemical rocket, an electric thruster does not obtain its main propulsive energy from burning fuel with an oxidiser.

A widely used method feeds an inert gas such as xenon into the thruster. Electrical energy converts some gas atoms into charged particles called ions. In Hall-effect and gridded ion thrusters, electric fields accelerate the ions out of the thruster. The escaping material provides thrust in the opposite direction. Hall-effect thrusters, also called stationary plasma thrusters in ISRO material, and gridded ion thrusters are 2 important examples. Their detailed construction is not needed to understand the principle.

Solar electric propulsion is not a solar sail. Solar panels provide electrical power to a thruster, which still uses and ejects propellant. A solar sail is a different system that gains momentum from sunlight without ejecting onboard propellant.

Why electric thrusters suit satellites

Electric thrusters can expel a small amount of propellant at very high speed. Their specific impulse is typically much higher than that of chemical thrusters, so they can perform many orbit corrections while carrying less propellant. Their trade-off is very low thrust: a single short firing makes only a small change in motion. The effect becomes useful when thrust continues or is repeated over long periods.

Electric propulsion is especially useful for station keeping, which means correcting small changes in a satellite's orbit; attitude-related manoeuvres where suitably configured thrusters help orient a spacecraft; and gradual orbit raising or transfer when a mission has sufficient time and electrical power. It is generally unsuitable as the principal system for lifting a large rocket directly from Earth's surface. Limited electrical power and long manoeuvre times are important constraints.

India's first flight example: GSAT-9

GSAT-9, the South Asia Satellite, was launched on 5 May 2017. It carried both chemical propulsion and plasma thrusters. The chemical Liquid Apogee Motor was used for initial orbit-raising manoeuvres; the electric thrusters assisted with station keeping. The electric propulsion system was therefore not the launch-vehicle engine or the satellite's only propulsion system.

LPSC developed an 18 millinewton (mN) stationary plasma thruster for north-south station keeping; the system was flown on GSAT-9. This shows why low-thrust electric propulsion can be valuable after a satellite has already reached space. As of the stated 2017 mission, GSAT-9's use of electric propulsion was an Indian flight demonstration, not evidence that all Indian launch vehicles use electric engines.

Prelims focus

  • Electric propulsion uses electricity to accelerate and expel propellant; it does not require chemical combustion.
  • Xenon is a commonly used inert-gas propellant; ions or plasma may be accelerated.
  • Electric propulsion normally has low thrust and high specific impulse.
  • Best-known applications include station keeping and gradual orbit adjustment.
  • GSAT-9 (5 May 2017) carried plasma thrusters to assist station keeping.
  • Trap: Electric propulsion still expels propellant; it is not simply movement produced by sunlight.

[NCERT, Science, Class 6, Chapter 12, 'Electricity and Circuits', printed pp. 116-122 (2018-19); NCERT, Science, Class 7, Chapter 14, 'Electric Current and its Effects', printed pp. 160-165 (2018-19); LPSC, 'Advanced Propulsion Systems', 'High Thrust Electric Propulsion (HEP) Project'; ISRO, 'GSAT-9', mission profile dated 5 May 2017; NASA, 'Solar Electric Propulsion', 'How SEP Works' (online sources consulted 4 November 2026).]

pictures.alt: Electricity powers ionisation and acceleration of xenon propellant; ions escape downward and the reaction force pushes the spacecraft upward, without combustion.
pictures.caption: Electrical power accelerates propellant; the escaping ions create thrust.

pictures.alt: Chemical rockets give high thrust briefly and use more propellant; electric thrusters give low thrust over longer periods with high specific impulse.
pictures.caption: Chemical and electric propulsion trade thrust against operating time and propellant use.

title: Electric propulsion: efficient, low-thrust movement in space

body:
What does green mean in rocket propellants?

In space propulsion, the term green propellant usually refers to a proposed or demonstrated alternative that aims to reduce toxicity, handling risks or harmful environmental effects compared with traditional propellants. It is a relative term, not a promise that a propellant is harmless. Handling concentrated chemicals and hot exhaust can still pose dangers.

Hydrazine and some related fuels have been widely used for satellite thrusters because they can be stored for long periods and produce thrust reliably. Their serious disadvantage is toxicity, which makes transport, fuelling and ground handling demanding. Green-propellant research tries to retain useful propulsion performance while reducing these risks.

Common alternative propellants

  • Hydrogen peroxide (H2O2): Can serve as a monopropellant or an oxidiser in certain alternative chemical systems. It is not harmless, especially in concentrated form.
  • Hydroxylammonium nitrate (HAN) formulations: Investigated as lower-toxicity alternatives for some chemical thrusters.
  • Ammonium dinitramide (ADN) formulations: Another class studied as an alternative to hydrazine-based monopropellants.

The words monopropellant and bipropellant describe how the chemical propellants are arranged, not whether they are green. A monopropellant stores 1 prepared propellant; a bipropellant system separately supplies a fuel and oxidiser. Green alternatives can be considered for either category.

Indian development and demonstration

ISRO's LPSC has reported development of 10 N and 100 N hydrogen-peroxide-based monopropellant thrusters, alongside work on alternatives to conventional toxic propellants. Research on HAN and ADN does not by itself establish that every such formulation has entered routine operational use.

ISRO's POEM-4 (PS4 Orbital Experiment Module) payload list, published on 22 December 2024 for the PSLV-C60/SpaDeX mission, included VYOM-2U, a proposed hydrogen-peroxide-based green monopropellant thruster developed by Manastu Space Technologies, Mumbai. It was described as a technology demonstration, with a designed thrust of about 1.1 N. The same payload list included the RUDRA 1.0 HPGP green-propulsion experiment from Bellatrix Aerospace, Bengaluru. A payload's listed aims must not be mistaken for independently verified operational performance.

Limits of the green label

Some LOX-based launch propellants, including LOX-kerosene, are described as cleaner than certain toxic older combinations. Nevertheless, burning a carbon-containing fuel can release carbon dioxide and other products. Green does not necessarily mean zero emissions, chemical-free propulsion or electric propulsion. An alternative can improve ground safety while still producing chemical exhaust.

Prelims focus

  • Green-propellant development aims mainly at lower toxicity and safer handling relative to hazardous conventional fuels.
  • Hydrazine is a common conventional but toxic spacecraft propellant.
  • Hydrogen peroxide, HAN and ADN are examples associated with alternative chemical propulsion.
  • LPSC reported hydrogen-peroxide monopropellant thrusters in 10 N and 100 N classes.
  • POEM-4's green-propulsion payloads included VYOM-2U (Manastu, Mumbai) and RUDRA 1.0 HPGP (Bellatrix, Bengaluru).
  • Trap: A green chemical thruster does not automatically operate without propellant, emissions or handling hazards.

[LPSC, 'Advanced Propulsion', 'Green Propulsion', ISRO-LPSC publication; LPSC, 'Research Areas', 'Alternate green propellants'; ISRO, 'POEM-4 in PSLV-C60 / SpaDeX Mission', 22 December 2024, payloads 'RUDRA 1.0 HPGP' and 'VYOM-2U'; NCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter 6, 'Combustion and Flame', printed pp. 73-74 (2018-19); NASA, 'Green Propellant Infusion Mission (GPIM) Overview', description of hydrazine alternatives (online sources consulted 4 November 2026).]

pictures.alt: Two technicians in protective equipment inspect a small satellite thruster secured on a workbench in a clean spacecraft integration area.
pictures.caption: Green-propellant work aims to reduce hazardous handling, not eliminate every risk.

pictures.alt: Lower-toxicity candidates can use 1 prepared monopropellant or separately stored fuel and oxidiser in a bipropellant system.

title: Green propellants: reducing toxic chemicals in spacecraft propulsion
